Sometimes I wonder if I’m stagnating because I’m working with in certain parameters, but also I feel like in terms of craftsmanship I’m growing. I’ve never really appreciated or understood production pottery or how you could make the same bowl or the same mug, and while this isn’t really that I am using some of the same building techniques the basic thing stays the same, and then it’s really just variables that create these characters, and I’m kind of enjoying the practice of it. #vermontartist #ceramics #scarymonster #kilnreveal

pricing my work is truly my LEAST favourite thing 😭  especially after trying to look closer at the numbers behind my small ceramic business. i’m trying to map out the potential 1, 3, and 5 year revenue and expense projections to see if investing in a kiln and building this business actually makes any sense. at my current $30-$65 price point, i’m losing money selling my work and cannot justify a kiln. i’ve made the terrifying decision to raise my prices by 25-30%. the money will go towards expanding production (investing. in a kiln & shelving), upgrading my website, expanding to ship to the US, and finally, offering private lessons and workshops.  with the price increase, I will still need to survive 6 months - 1 year without a livable wage / making profit. i’ll be focusing on my higher-margin petal bowls and bring in some more affordable $25 products like spoon rests and trinket dishes to keep things as accessible as possible. my mugs are not viable as they take me 2hrs each, but i’m going to keep making them for now and hope i can speed it up. no more lidded jars outside of speciality collections as the margins are too low.  i’m also going to try to secure 1-2 freelance social media clients to provide me with some supplement income as a buffer. this is the behind the scenes of small ceramics business’ that you normally don’t see, because it’s not nearly as cute or fun as the pots themselves. #potterybusiness #ceramics #smallbusiness #priceincrease #handmadeceramics

videos.caption: It’s been some time since I last returned to the slow, methodical business of clay testing, but this week I found myself back there again, working through a small series of black stoneware tests using a new body sent to me by Valentine Clays. The timing felt appropriate, a brief pause in the year where the workshop can become a place for looking closely rather than producing quickly. The clay is called Schwarz, a name that leaves little to the imagination, and one that was repeatedly suggested when I previously spoke about my ongoing search for a genuinely black clay body that behaved. It contains 25% grog, yet in the hands it feels unexpectedly smooth, this is explained by the minute particle size, which is extremely fine at around 0.02 mm. The result is a body that throws cleanly, trims crisply, and carries its edges with confidence whilst still retaining the structural benefits that grog can provide. There’s a reassuring density to it as you work, and a sense that it wants to hold its form rather than collapse into softness. That said, no clay arrives without its compromises. The maximum firing temperature is listed at 1240ºC, which sits some way below the cone ten firings that my work is normally pushed to. Rather than dismissing it outright, I’m more interested in seeing how it behaves when blended with higher-firing bodies, and whether its colour and strength can survive a reduction firing up to 1290ºC. Over the coming weeks I’ll be mixing, testing, and firing a range of variations, paying close attention to how the black responds, and whether the pots retain their intended geometry once they’ve passed through the kiln. As ever, the answers lie less in assumptions and more in repetition, observation, and time. Thanks very much for watching and if you’d like to see a more exploratory video that discusses the entirety of the throwing and trimming, you can find a link to longer video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography. #pottery #ceramics #clay #stoneware #handmade

In my YouTube video this weekend I’m recreating some pots I haven’t thrown since 2014, specially store jars with inset, internal galleries and thin lids with thrown knobs. You can find a link to the fully narrated video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   I’ve lied a little bit. I did create jars that were similar to this during my apprenticeship with Lisa Hammond between 2014-2017, yet they were bellied pieces with a gallery closer to the jars I make these days, yet they unusual thrown knobs that were in themselves similar to small bowls.   To create pots with internal galleries like this you need to split the rim. One section becomes the lip, the other is coaxed inside and carefully set horizontal to essentially become a ledge onto which the lid can be held aloft. This alone is a tricky task and it involves throwing a form with enough material in the lip to withstand such a manoeuvre. Secondly, there’s the small disc-like lid, a form that’s thrown off-the-hump and then the following day it’s trimmed back to have its more exacting shape and the knob is thrown on, again, a tricky task as it involves fiddly, fingertip throwing and a lot of accuracy.   All of this and more will be covered in my longer, narrated YouTube upload. I enjoyed making these and since it has been such a long time since I’ve crafted them, my skillset in the interim has improved massively, thus I could apply newly learnt techniques and ability into making shapes I used to struggle with to some degree. I hope you like the film if you happen to click over and watch it, it’s greatly appreciated if you do as it helps to keep the lights on in the workshop.   #pottery #ceramics #handmade #jar #satisfying

videos.caption: Here’s a completed apothecary jar and a full overview of how it’s made. For this type of lidded jar, the base and lid are thrown from one continuous piece of clay, then cut open and trimmed to create the inner edges and gallery so the lid doesn’t slide off. I like this type of piece because it has a continuous line from the base to the top of the knob. It’s a very elegant shape and one I imagine would look lovely on a shelf holding trinkets, spices, or chocolates. #pottery #studioceramics #wheelthrown #handmade #potteryartist

This short video is just a snippet from my film length YouTube video this weekend that shows the entire creation of these mugs from beginning to end in excruciating detail. It’s an hour and ten-minutes long and you can find a link to the fully narrated video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography. It might be the longest film I’ve created yet, stitched together from footage filmed and accumulated over the past two-years. It shows how I create one of my simple, handmade ceramic mugs, from beginning to end, with every single fleeting step in that process included. These vessels are amongst the pots I’ve made the most of yet there’s still subtle variations that creep into each batch. Despite the form being immensely simple, there's endless minute details that go into creating any pot thousands of times. Over the years a potter will finesse their practice, figuring out new efficiencies, improvements and ways of speeding up the making process. I’ve always found chatting about these seemingly unnoticeable actions with other craftspeople fascinating and so I hope some of what I’ve learnt over the past fifteen years is helpful to anybody who decides to sit through this. Ultimately, being a production potter isn't all about speed, as quality can't be sacrificed for haste. This means there's a point if you're making repetitively, or learning to, when your speed will lessen as you focus on keeping the quality of the thrown items top-notch. Then, as you sink hundreds of hours into practicing a particular shape, the faster you'll become whilst being able to retain a certain level of quality. It's this tireless persistence that many potters I know have, which helps them become really fluid throwers, trimmers and handlers of pots. Beyond those steps, I've tried to discuss the glazing, firing and the steps taken after the vessels have been plucked out of the kiln in greater detail, as I really want to try and paint a thorough picture of what it really means to make pottery like this and on this scale.  If you happen to watch the full video, please do let me know! Enjoy! #pottery #mug #handmade #ceramics #satisfying
